title: Bringing Back the Dead
principle: Trying to bring an extinct animal back is called de-extinction.

t: DNA falls apart at a rate you can measure. That single fact decides what can and cannot be brought back.
Ancient DNA degrades with a measurable half-life, so the question of which extinct species are recoverable has an arithmetic answer rather than an aspirational one.
sub: It is not about how clever anyone is.
The limit is chemistry, and it was quantified from a pile of bird bones.

stages.label: How long ago did it die?
captions: A museum specimen from 1900: the whole genome, easily read.
A mammoth frozen 40,000 years ago: nearly all of it, in short broken pieces.
A mammoth tooth in permafrost, over a million years old: fragments, and the oldest DNA anyone has ever read.
Two million years, from frozen Greenland mud: scraps, and only because it never thawed.
A dinosaur, 66 million years ago: nothing at all. There is no technique, because there is nothing left to read.
t: Slide back through time and watch how much of the instructions survive.
The recovery limit, established empirically. Note that the last step is not a difficulty — it is an absence.
after: The film was never going to happen, and now you know exactly why.

Measurements on hundreds of dated bones give a half-life of about 520 years for a short fragment under cool conditions. Applied forward, every bond is broken well before a million years at moderate temperature; permafrost extends it, and nothing extends it to 66 million.

t: Bring something back. Any part fits any slot, so the marking is on you.
Assign each requirement, then five tests. The last one is the one the field argues about.

label: The instructions, recovered well enough to use
A genome close enough to edit rather than write
A body that can carry it to birth
A place that still has what it needs
The animals it would have learned from

name: Read the instructions
Sequence
pass: Enough of the genome has been recovered to work from.
Sufficient coverage assembled from overlapping degraded fragments.
fail: Too little survives to reconstruct anything.
Below a threshold of coverage, gaps cannot be bridged and the sequence is not usable.

name: Put them in something living
Host genome
pass: A close relative's genome is edited towards the extinct one.
Targeted edits at loci of interest, in the closest extant genome available.
fail: Nobody can write a whole genome from scratch and boot it in an animal.
Synthesis at that scale has been achieved only in bacteria. For an animal the only route is editing a relative.

name: Get it born
Development
pass: A surrogate carries it, or an artificial womb does.
Somatic cell nuclear transfer into an enucleated egg, implanted in a surrogate of the related species.
fail: An edited cell in a dish is not an animal.
This step is where almost every attempt has failed. The one extinct animal ever born — a Pyrenean ibex, in 2003 — lived for seven minutes.

name: Keep it alive
Habitat
pass: The place it needs still exists.
Habitat availability is a precondition, and for most extinct species it is the binding one.
fail: An animal with nowhere to be.
Most species went extinct because their habitat did. Reversing the animal does not reverse the cause.

name: Have it actually be a mammoth
Identity
pass: A population, raised by others of its kind.
Behaviour in long-lived social species is culturally transmitted; a founder generation has nobody to learn from.
fail: You have an elephant with cold-weather genes and nobody to teach it how to be a mammoth.

This is the honest description of what current approaches would produce: an edited elephant with some mammoth traits, raised without mammoth behaviour. Whether that counts is a definitional question, and it should be asked before the work rather than after.

win: Instructions, a relative, a birth, a home and a herd. Only the first three are technical problems.
All five. Note the shape of it: the biology is the tractable part. Habitat and transmitted behaviour are not solved by any amount of sequencing, and they are where the concept actually breaks.
lose: Read which test failed — it names what was missing.
Each failed trial names an unmet requirement. Reassign and re-test.

t: Trying to bring an extinct animal back is called de-extinction. What comes back is a very good copy.
De-extinction produces an approximation. The routes are back-breeding, cloning from an intact cell, and editing a close relative's genome — and only the third is available for anything long dead.

The recovered sequence is assembled from millions of short damaged fragments, mapped against a living relative's genome to work out where they go. That reference is doing a great deal of the work, so the result is partly the relative by construction.

This makes the word 'back' the contested part rather than the technique. An Asian elephant edited at several dozen loci for cold tolerance is a real and difficult achievement and is not a mammoth; it shares 99.6% of its genome with Asian elephants because it is one. Whether an approximation that fills the same ecological role counts as the species returning is a question about what a species is, and it is being answered implicitly by press release rather than explicitly by argument.
sub: You cannot copy something you cannot read all of.
The gaps in an ancient genome get filled in from the nearest living relative, because there is nothing else to fill them from.
Which means the closer the relative, the better the result and the less of the extinct animal it contains.

The genuinely useful spin-off is not disputed by anyone: the same cloning and biobanking work has produced living black-footed ferrets and Przewalski's horses from decades-old frozen cells, adding genetic diversity to populations too inbred to recover on their own. That is de-extinction technique applied to species that are not extinct, and it is working.

q: Why can nobody bring back a dinosaur?
Why is 66 million years beyond any recovery technique?
Why does the reference genome make 'bringing back' an imprecise description?
options: DNA falls apart, and after that long there is none left to read
No living relative is close enough
why: DNA breaks itself apart slowly no matter what you do. After a few million years there are no pieces left big enough to read, and after 66 million there is nothing at all.

The measured half-life implies complete fragmentation well within a few million years even in permafrost. There is no signal remaining to amplify, so the limit is the absence of material rather than the sensitivity of the method.

Because the gaps in a degraded genome are filled from the closest living relative, so a fraction of the reconstruction is that relative's sequence rather than the extinct animal's. The recovered genome is a mosaic whose composition depends on how much survived — which means the phrase describes a spectrum, not an event.

t: The same techniques are keeping living species from going extinct in the first place.

Frozen cells from animals that died in the 1980s have produced living, breeding black-footed ferrets carrying genetic variation the surviving population had lost. That is the strongest argument the field has: whatever one concludes about mammoths, the tools are demonstrably useful on animals that are still here.
